decks.title: Circular Motion — Part 1: Angular quantities and centripetal acceleration
goals: Define angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration, and use s = rθ, v = rω and a_t = rα
Explain why a body moving on a circle at constant speed is accelerated
Derive a = v²/r = ω²r from the change in velocity, and show that it points to the centre
Treat centripetal force as the name of a direction, and name the real force that supplies it

slides.narration: A ceiling fan, a potter wheel and a satellite all go round in circles. How fast is a point on the blade going, and why does a stone on a string pull on your hand? In this part we describe motion on a circle using angles, link them to ordinary speed, and then find the acceleration that every circular motion needs.

slides.heading: Angular displacement and the radian
slides.body_md: The **angular displacement** $\theta$ of a body on a circle is the angle swept by the line joining it to the centre. The SI unit is the **radian**: the angle at the centre for an arc equal in length to the radius.
bullets: A full turn is $2\pi$ rad $= 360^\circ$, so $1\ \text{rad} = 57.30^\circ$. The radian is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no dimensions.
In the first figure, on the title slide, $r = 2$ m and $\theta = 0.9$ rad, so the arc is $s = 2 \times 0.9 = 1.80$ m.
Anticlockwise turning is taken as positive. The angular displacement is a vector along the axis, found by the right-hand rule.

rows: Angle for an arc of 1.8 m on r = 2.0 m

visual.alt: Table of angles in degrees and radians: full turn, half turn, quarter turn, one radian, and the angle for an arc of 1.8 metres on a circle of radius 2.0 metres

slides.narration: Angular displacement is the angle swept by the line from the centre to the body. Its unit is the radian, the angle for which the arc is as long as the radius. So the arc length equals the radius times the angle in radians. One full turn is two pi radians, which is three hundred and sixty degrees. In the first figure, an arc of one point eight metres on a circle of radius two metres is point nine radians.

slides.heading: Angular velocity
slides.body_md: The **angular velocity** is the rate of change of angular displacement. For a steady turn at frequency $f$, or period $T$:
bullets: Unit: rad s$^{-1}$. In the first figure, $\omega = 0.9/0.6 = 1.50$ rad s$^{-1}$.
Direction: along the axis, by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers the way the body turns and the thumb gives the direction of $\omega$.
Revolutions per minute convert as $\omega = 2\pi \times \text{rpm}/60$.

visual.alt: Table of angular speeds in radians per second for the second, minute and hour hands of a clock, the rotation of the Earth and the revolution of the Moon, each from 2 pi over the period

slides.narration: Angular velocity is how fast the angle changes. For a steady turn it is two pi divided by the period, or two pi times the frequency. Its unit is radians per second, and its direction is along the axis, given by the right hand rule. To convert revolutions per minute, multiply by two pi and divide by sixty. The table shows some familiar rotations, from the second hand of a clock to the Earth.

slides.heading: Linear speed and angular speed: v = rω
slides.body_md: In a time $\Delta t$ the body moves along an arc $\Delta s = r\Delta\theta$. Dividing by $\Delta t$:
bullets: The velocity is along the **tangent**, perpendicular to the radius.
Every point of a rotating rigid body has the **same** $\omega$, but the speed $v = r\omega$ grows with the distance from the axis.
On a merry-go-round the child on the outer seat travels faster, yet turns through the same angle in the same time.

visual.alt: Table for three seats on a merry-go-round turning at 0.80 radians per second: the angular speed is the same for all, while the speed and the centripetal acceleration grow with the distance from the axis

math: v = \dfrac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = r\,\dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = r\omega
slides.narration: From the arc length, divide the arc covered by the time taken. The arc is r times the angle, so the speed is r times the angular velocity. The velocity points along the tangent. Every point of a rotating body has the same angular velocity, but points farther from the axis move faster. On a merry go round, all the seats turn through the same angle, but the outer seat covers a longer path.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a potter’s wheel
slides.body_md: A potter’s wheel of radius $0.3$ m turns at $75$ revolutions per minute. Find its angular speed, the period, and the speed of a point on the rim and of a point $0.1$ m from the axis.
bullets: Nearer the axis: $v = 0.1 \times 7.854 = 0.7854$ m s$^{-1}$: one third of the radius, one third of the speed.

rows: Speed at 0.1 m from the axis

visual.alt: Table of the working for a potter wheel at 75 revolutions per minute: angular speed, period, rim speed and speed nearer the axis

slides.narration: Seventy five revolutions per minute is seventy five times two pi over sixty, which is seven point eight five four radians per second. The period is point eight seconds. The rim, at point three metres, moves at two point three five six metres per second. A point at point one metre moves at zero point seven eight five four metres per second, one third as fast, because its radius is one third.

slides.heading: Angular acceleration
slides.body_md: The **angular acceleration** is the rate of change of angular velocity, $\alpha = \Delta\omega/\Delta t$ (or $d\omega/dt$). Unit: rad s$^{-2}$. For constant $\alpha$:
bullets: On an $\omega$–$t$ graph the **slope** is $\alpha$ and the **area** under the line is $\theta$.
A fan starting from rest with $\alpha = 2.5$ rad s$^{-2}$ reaches $\omega = 20.0$ rad s$^{-1}$ in $8$ s, having turned through $\theta = 80.0$ rad.
If $\omega$ is steady, $\alpha = 0$ and the circular motion is uniform.

functions.label: ω = αt with α = 2.5 rad s⁻²

visual.alt: Angular speed against time for a fan starting from rest with angular acceleration 2.5 radians per second squared: a straight line through the origin reaching 20 radians per second at 8 seconds; the area under the line is the angular displacement, 80 radians
visual.caption: The slope of the ω–t line is α; the area under it is θ.

slides.narration: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, in radians per second squared. For a constant value, the angular velocity grows as alpha times t, and the angle turned is half alpha t squared when starting from rest. On the graph, the slope is alpha and the area is the angle. A fan with two point five radians per second squared reaches twenty radians per second in eight seconds.

slides.heading: Tangential acceleration: a_t = rα
slides.body_md: Differentiating $v = r\omega$ with $r$ fixed gives the rate at which the **speed** changes along the circle:
bullets: This acceleration is along the **tangent**; it changes the speed, not the direction.
It is zero in uniform circular motion. The other part, $a_c = \omega^2 r$, always points to the centre and is the subject of the next slides.

visual.alt: Table linking angular and linear quantities: displacement, velocity, tangential acceleration and radial acceleration with the relations s equals r theta, v equals r omega, tangential a equals r alpha and centripetal a equals omega squared r

slides.narration: Taking the rate of change of v equals r omega, the rate of change of speed is r times alpha. This is the tangential acceleration. It acts along the tangent and changes the speed, not the direction. In uniform circular motion it is zero. A second acceleration, always pointing to the centre, is needed to turn the velocity, and we study it next.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a fan blade tip
slides.body_md: A fan blade tip is $0.6$ m from the axis. The fan starts from rest and speeds up with $\alpha = 2.5$ rad s$^{-2}$ for $8$ s. Find $\omega$, the angle turned, the tangential acceleration and the centripetal acceleration of the tip at the end of this time.
bullets: $\omega = \alpha t = 2.5 \times 8 = 20.0$ rad s$^{-1}$. $\theta = \tfrac12 \alpha t^2 = 80.0$ rad $= 12.7$ turns.
$a_c = \omega^2 r = 20.0^2 \times 0.6 = 240.0$ m s$^{-2}$, far larger; the total is $\sqrt{a_t^2 + a_c^2} = 240.00$ m s$^{-2}$.

visual.alt: Table of the working for a fan blade tip of radius 0.60 metres starting from rest with angular acceleration 2.5 radians per second squared for 8 seconds: angular speed, angular displacement, tangential, centripetal and total acceleration

slides.narration: After eight seconds the angular speed is twenty radians per second and the angle turned is eighty radians, about twelve point seven turns. The tangential acceleration is point six times two point five, one point five metres per second squared. The centripetal acceleration is two hundred and forty metres per second squared, which is far larger, so the total is almost the same as the centripetal part.

slides.heading: Uniform circular motion is accelerated
slides.body_md: In **uniform circular motion** the speed is constant, $\alpha = 0$ and $a_t = 0$. Yet the body is **accelerated**.
bullets: Velocity is a vector. Its **direction** keeps changing as the body goes round, so the velocity changes.
A change of velocity means an acceleration, even when the speed is steady.
Which way does that acceleration point, and how big is it? The velocity triangle on the next slides answers both.

rows: constant in size, to the centre
changes with ω, to the centre

visual.alt: Table comparing uniform and non-uniform circular motion: angular speed, speed, tangential acceleration, centripetal acceleration and total acceleration

slides.narration: In uniform circular motion the speed is steady, so there is no tangential acceleration. But velocity is a vector, and its direction keeps changing. A change in velocity is an acceleration, even when the speed does not change. So the body is accelerated. Which way does this acceleration point, and how large is it? The velocity triangle answers both questions.

slides.heading: The change in velocity: a triangle
slides.body_md: Take two points P and Q, a small angle $\Delta\theta$ apart. The speed $v$ is the same at both, but the velocities $\vec v_1$ and $\vec v_2$ are tangents at different directions.
bullets: Draw $\vec v_1$ and $\vec v_2$ from one point. The angle between them is $\Delta\theta$, the angle POQ, because each is perpendicular to its radius.
The change in velocity $\Delta\vec v = \vec v_2 - \vec v_1$ closes the triangle. It is the base of an **isosceles triangle** with two sides of length $v$.
For the figure, $v = 5$ m s$^{-1}$ and $\Delta\theta = 50^\circ$ give $|\Delta v| = 2v\sin(\Delta\theta/2) = 4.23$ m s$^{-1}$, pointing from the chord midpoint towards O.

slides.narration: Take two points on the circle, a small angle apart. The speeds are equal, but the velocities point in different directions along the tangents. Draw both from one point. The angle between them equals the angle at the centre, because each is perpendicular to its radius. The change in velocity joins their tips, the base of an isosceles triangle, and it points towards the centre.

slides.heading: Derivation: a = v²/r
slides.body_md: For a very small $\Delta\theta$ the base of the isosceles triangle equals the arc of radius $v$: $|\Delta v| \approx v\,\Delta\theta$.
bullets: As $\Delta\theta \to 0$, the angles at the base of the triangle approach $90^\circ$, so $\Delta\vec v$ becomes perpendicular to $\vec v$, that is **along the radius, towards the centre**.
This is the **centripetal acceleration**: constant in size, but changing in direction as the body goes round.
Using $\omega = 2\pi/T$: $a = 4\pi^2 r/T^2$.

math: a = \dfrac{|\Delta v|}{\Delta t} = v\,\dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} = v\omega, \qquad a = v\omega = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r
slides.narration: For a very small angle, the base of the triangle is nearly an arc of radius v, so the size of the change in velocity is v times the small angle. Divide by the small time, and the angle over time is omega. So the acceleration is v omega, which is v squared over r, which is omega squared r. As the angle shrinks to zero, the change in velocity points along the radius, towards the centre.

slides.heading: How the centripetal acceleration scales
slides.body_md: Because $a = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$, what is held fixed matters.
bullets: At **fixed $r$**: doubling $v$ makes $a$ four times larger.
At **fixed $v$**: $a \propto 1/r$. A sharper bend (smaller $r$) needs a larger acceleration.
At **fixed $\omega$**: $a \propto r$. Points far from the axis of a spinning disc accelerate more.
In the graph the two curves cross where $v = \omega r$.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a cyclist on a roundabout
slides.body_md: A cyclist and cycle of total mass $70$ kg go round a circular roundabout of radius $12$ m at a steady $6.0$ m s$^{-1}$. Find the centripetal acceleration and the force towards the centre.
bullets: $a = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \dfrac{6^2}{12} = 3.00$ m s$^{-2}$, towards the centre.
Check: $\omega = v/r = 0.500$ rad s$^{-1}$ and $\omega^2 r = 3.00$ m s$^{-2}$.
$F = ma = 70 \times 3.00 = 210$ N, directed to the centre. It is supplied by friction between the tyres and the road.

slides.narration: The centripetal acceleration is the speed squared over the radius, thirty six over twelve, which is three metres per second squared. Using angular velocity, point five radians per second, gives the same result. The force towards the centre is seventy times three, which is two hundred and ten newtons. Friction between the tyres and the road supplies it.

slides.heading: Centripetal force: a name for a direction
slides.body_md: By Newton’s second law, a body with centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$ needs a **net force towards the centre** of size $F = mv^2/r = m\omega^2 r$.
bullets: **Centripetal force** is not a new kind of force. It is the **name of a direction**: it describes whichever real force, or combination of forces, points to the centre.
On a free-body diagram show only the real forces: tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction. **Never add a separate arrow** called centripetal force.
The sum of the real forces towards the centre must equal $mv^2/r$.
It is perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion and does no work on the body.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a stone on a table
slides.body_md: A stone of mass $0.25$ kg is whirled on a smooth horizontal table by a string of length $0.8$ m at $2$ revolutions per second. Find the tension. What is the greatest frequency if the string breaks at $50$ N?
bullets: The tension is the only horizontal force, so $T = m\omega^2 r = 0.25 \times 12.57^2 \times 0.8 = 31.58$ N.
At the limit, $\omega_{\max} = \sqrt{T/(mr)} = 15.81$ rad s$^{-1}$, so $f_{\max} = 2.516$ rev s$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: Two revolutions per second is twelve point five seven radians per second. The string tension is the only force along the radius, so it equals mass times omega squared times radius, thirty one point five eight newtons. A string that breaks at fifty newtons allows an angular velocity of fifteen point eight one radians per second, which is two point five one six revolutions per second.

slides.narration: To sum up. Angular displacement is s over r in radians. Angular velocity is two pi over the period. The speed is r times omega, along the tangent, and the tangential acceleration is r times alpha. A body in uniform circular motion has a centripetal acceleration of v squared over r towards the centre. Centripetal force names that direction; a real force such as tension, friction or gravity supplies it.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Convert revolutions per minute to rad s⁻¹ by multiplying by $2\pi/60$ before using $v = r\omega$.

For the derivation of $a = v^2/r$ draw both velocity vectors from one point, mark the angle $\Delta\theta$, show $|\Delta v| \approx v\Delta\theta$ and say the direction is towards the centre as $\Delta\theta \to 0$.
Name the real force that supplies the centripetal force; never draw "centripetal force" as an extra arrow on the free-body diagram.
Centripetal acceleration is $v^2/r$, tangential acceleration is $r\alpha$: do not mix them up, and add them as vectors at right angles.
Common mistakes: using degrees in $s = r\theta$; saying the acceleration is zero because the speed is constant; saying centripetal force does work on the body.

slides.narration: Why does a car skid on a wet bend? Why are expressway curves tilted, and why is the outer rail of a railway curve higher? And how can a bucket of water be swung over your head without spilling? In this part we use the centripetal force idea for roads, tracks and vertical circles.

slides.heading: A vehicle on a level curve
slides.body_md: On a **level** road the only horizontal force on the car is the **friction** between the tyres and the road. It points to the centre of the curve and **is** the centripetal force.
bullets: The tyres grip without sliding sideways, so this is **static** friction, with a largest value $\mu N$.
There is no vertical acceleration, so $N = mg$.
If the friction needed, $mv^2/r$, would exceed $\mu mg$, the car skids outwards along the tangent.

slides.narration: On a level bend the only horizontal force on the car is friction between the tyres and the road. It points to the centre, so friction supplies the centripetal force. It is static friction, because the tyres do not slide sideways, and it has a largest value, mu times N. The normal reaction equals the weight. If more friction is needed than the road can give, the car skids outwards.

slides.heading: The greatest safe speed: v_max = √(μrg)
slides.body_md: At the limit, the friction needed equals the greatest friction available:
bullets: The **mass cancels**: a loaded truck and a small car on the same road have the same $v_{\max}$ (the greatest friction and the needed force are both proportional to $m$).
A larger $\mu$ or a larger radius allows a higher speed; a **wet** road (smaller $\mu$) lowers it.

visual.alt: Table of the steps for the greatest speed on a level curve: vertical balance, needed inward force, friction limit, combining them and the result v at most the square root of mu r g

slides.narration: At the limit, the friction needed, m v squared over r, equals the greatest friction available, mu times m g. The mass cancels, so the greatest safe speed is the square root of mu r g. A truck and a car on the same bend have the same limit. A bigger radius or a larger coefficient allows a higher speed, and a wet road with a smaller coefficient lowers it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a bend in the rain
slides.body_md: A bend of radius $45$ m is level. Find the greatest safe speed on a dry road ($\mu = 0.7$) and on a wet road ($\mu = 0.35$). Take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.
bullets: $\mu$ halved, so $v_{\max}$ falls by the factor $\sqrt{1/2} = 0.707$, not by one half.

visual.alt: Table of the greatest safe speed on a level curve of radius 45 metres for dry, wet and icy road with coefficients of friction 0.70, 0.35 and 0.10

slides.narration: On the dry road, the greatest speed is the square root of zero point seven times forty five times nine point eight, which is seventeen point five seven metres per second. On the wet road, with the coefficient halved, it is twelve point four two metres per second. Halving the coefficient reduces the greatest speed by the square root of one half, about seventy one per cent of the dry value.

slides.heading: Why bank the road?
slides.body_md: Friction is limited, wears the tyres and nearly vanishes on a wet or oily road. A **banked** road tilts towards the **inside** of the bend (the outer edge is higher), so the **normal reaction** itself has a horizontal part pointing to the centre.
bullets: The normal reaction is perpendicular to the **road**, not to the ground, so it leans towards the centre.
Its vertical part balances the weight; its horizontal part is the centripetal force.
At the **design speed** no friction is needed at all.

slides.narration: Friction is limited and nearly disappears on a wet road. So bends are banked, with the outer edge higher. The normal reaction is perpendicular to the road, so it leans towards the centre of the bend. Its vertical part balances the weight, and its horizontal part supplies the centripetal force. At the design speed, no friction is needed at all.

slides.heading: Derivation: tan θ = v²/(rg)
slides.body_md: A car of mass $m$ moves at speed $v$ on a bend of radius $r$, banked at angle $\theta$, with no friction needed.
bullets: Divide the second equation by the first: $N$ and $m$ cancel, so the angle depends only on $v$ and $r$.
The **design speed** for a given $\theta$ is $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.
The mass does not appear: heavy and light vehicles need the same banking.

rows: Design speed for a given θ
Figure: v = 20 m s⁻¹, r = 100 m

visual.alt: Table of the steps for the banking angle: vertical balance, horizontal equation, dividing to get tan theta equals v squared over r g, the design speed and the numbers for 20 metres per second on a curve of radius 100 metres

slides.narration: Resolve the normal reaction. Its vertical part balances the weight, N cos theta equals m g. Its horizontal part gives the centripetal force, N sin theta equals m v squared over r. Divide the second equation by the first. The normal reaction and the mass cancel, leaving tan theta equal to v squared over r g. The mass does not appear, so all vehicles use the same banking.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an expressway curve
slides.body_md: A curve of radius $100$ m is to be banked for $20$ m s$^{-1}$ ($72.0$ km h$^{-1}$). Find the angle of banking, and the normal reaction on a car of mass $800$ kg moving at that speed. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg} = \dfrac{20^2}{100 \times 9.8} = 0.4082$, so $\theta = 22.20^\circ$.
$N = \dfrac{mg}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{800 \times 9.8}{\cos 22.2^\circ} = 8468$ N.
Check: $N\sin\theta = 3200$ N $= mv^2/r = 3200$ N.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the banking angle of a curve of radius 100 metres at 20 metres per second: tan theta, theta, the normal reaction for an 800 kilogram car and a check

slides.narration: The tangent of the angle is the speed squared over r g, four hundred over nine hundred and eighty, which is zero point four zero eight two. So the angle is twenty two point two degrees. The normal reaction is the weight divided by the cosine, eight thousand four hundred and sixty eight newtons. As a check, its horizontal part is three thousand two hundred newtons, equal to m v squared over r.

slides.heading: Railway tracks: raise the outer rail
slides.body_md: On a railway curve the **outer rail is raised** above the inner rail, so the track is banked. The flanges of the wheels then need not press sideways on the rails at the design speed.
bullets: If the gauge (distance between the rails, measured along the sleeper) is $l$ and the outer rail is $h$ higher, $\sin\theta = h/l$.
$\theta$ is small, so $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta$ and $h \approx l\,\dfrac{v^2}{rg}$.
Too fast: the train presses on the outer rail. Too slow: on the inner rail. Either wears the rail and the wheel flange.

slides.narration: On a railway curve, the outer rail is raised above the inner rail. If the gap between the rails is l and the height difference is h, then sine theta is h over l. For a small angle, sine and tangent are almost equal, so h is about l times v squared over r g. At the design speed the wheels do not push sideways on either rail. A faster or slower train presses on one rail.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: raising the outer rail
slides.body_md: A curve of radius $500$ m on a broad-gauge line ($l = 1.676$ m) is designed for $20$ m s$^{-1}$ ($72.0$ km h$^{-1}$). By how much must the outer rail be raised?
bullets: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{20^2}{500 \times 9.8} = 0.08163$, so $\theta = 4.667^\circ$.
$h = l\sin\theta = 1.676 \times 0.081362 = 0.1364$ m, about $136$ mm.
The approximation $h \approx l\tan\theta = 0.1368$ m differs by less than one per cent.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the raised outer rail on a curve of radius 500 metres for 20 metres per second and a gauge of 1.676 metres: tan theta, sin theta, h equal to l sin theta and the approximation l tan theta

slides.narration: The tangent of the angle is zero point zero eight one six three, so the angle is about four point six seven degrees. The height is the gauge, one point six seven six metres, times the sine of the angle, which is zero point one three six four metres, about one hundred and thirty six millimetres. The approximation using the tangent gives almost the same, zero point one three six eight metres.

slides.heading: Other speeds on a banked track
slides.body_md: The banking angle is built for **one** design speed. The graph shows how steeply the angle rises with $v$.
bullets: Above the design speed the vehicle tends to move **outwards** and up the slope; friction, or the outer rail, must supply the extra inward force.
Below it the vehicle tends to slide **inwards** and down the slope; friction, or the inner rail, holds it.
Because $\tan\theta \propto v^2$, doubling the speed on the same curve needs about four times the value of $\tan\theta$.

visual.alt: Banking angle against design speed for a curve of radius 100 metres: the angle rises from zero, reaching 5.8 degrees at 10 metres per second and 22.2 degrees at 20 metres per second, and grows steeply at higher speed
visual.caption: Doubling the speed far more than doubles the angle needed: tan θ ∝ v².

slides.narration: A banked track is built for one design speed. Above that speed, a vehicle tends to move outwards and up the slope, so friction or the outer rail supplies the extra inward force. Below it, the vehicle tends to slide inwards and down. Because tan theta grows as the square of the speed, doubling the speed needs about four times the tangent of the angle.

slides.heading: Motion in a vertical circle
slides.body_md: A ball on a string moves in a **vertical** circle. Gravity speeds it up as it falls and slows it as it rises, so this motion is **not uniform**: the speed is least at the top and greatest at the bottom.
bullets: The weight acts downwards throughout; the tension acts along the string, **towards the centre**.
At every point, (force towards the centre) $= mv^2/r$.
At the **top** both $T$ and $mg$ point to the centre; at the **bottom** $T$ points to the centre and $mg$ points away.

slides.narration: In a vertical circle, gravity speeds the ball up as it falls and slows it as it rises, so the speed is least at the top and greatest at the bottom. The weight always acts downwards and the tension acts along the string towards the centre. At every point the net force towards the centre is m v squared over r. At the top, tension and weight both point to the centre. At the bottom, only the tension does.

slides.heading: The least speed at the top: √(gr)
slides.body_md: At the **top**, $T$ and $mg$ both point to the centre:
bullets: A string can only pull, so $T \ge 0$. The **least speed** has $T = 0$: the weight alone supplies the centripetal force.
$mg = \dfrac{mv_{\min}^2}{r} \Rightarrow v_{\text{top,min}} = \sqrt{gr}$.
Slower than this, the string goes slack and the ball leaves the circle and falls inside it.

slides.narration: At the top, the tension and the weight both point to the centre. A string can only pull, so the tension cannot be negative. The least speed is when the tension is zero, and the weight alone supplies the centripetal force. Then g equals v squared over r, so the least speed at the top is the square root of g r. Slower than this, the string goes slack.

slides.heading: The least speed at the bottom: √(5gr)
slides.body_md: From the top to the bottom the ball falls through $2r$. Mechanical energy is conserved (gravity is the only force that does work; the tension is perpendicular to the motion):
bullets: With the least top speed $v_{\text{top}}^2 = gr$: $v_{\text{bot}}^2 = 5gr$, so $v_{\text{bot,min}} = \sqrt{5gr}$.
For the figure, $r = 0.9$ m: $\sqrt{gr} = 2.97$ m s$^{-1}$ and $\sqrt{5gr} = 6.64$ m s$^{-1}$.
A ball launched from the bottom slower than $\sqrt{5gr}$ cannot complete the circle.

slides.narration: From top to bottom the ball falls a height of two r. Mechanical energy is conserved, because only gravity does work. So the speed squared at the bottom is the speed squared at the top plus four g r. With the least top speed, speed squared at the top is g r, so the bottom speed squared is five g r. The least speed at the bottom is the square root of five g r.

slides.heading: Tension at the bottom and at the top
slides.body_md: At the **bottom**, $T$ points to the centre and $mg$ points away:
bullets: Subtract and use $v_{\text{bot}}^2 = v_{\text{top}}^2 + 4gr$: $T_{\text{bot}} - T_{\text{top}} = 6mg$ **for any speed**.
At the least speed: $T_{\text{top}} = 0$ and $T_{\text{bot}} = 6mg$. For the figure that is $29.4$ N.
The string is most likely to snap at the **bottom**, where the tension is greatest.

slides.narration: At the bottom, the tension points to the centre and the weight points away, so tension minus m g equals m v squared over r. At the top, tension plus m g equals m v squared over r. Subtracting, and using the energy result, the bottom tension is always six m g more than the top tension. At the least speed the top tension is zero and the bottom tension is six m g.

slides.body_md: A bucket and water of total mass $2$ kg is whirled on a rope of length $1.6$ m in a vertical circle. Find the least speed at the top and at the bottom, the rope tension at the bottom for that case, and the tension at the top when the speed there is $5.0$ m s$^{-1}$. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: $v_{\text{top,min}} = \sqrt{gr} = 3.960$ m s$^{-1}$ and $v_{\text{bot,min}} = \sqrt{5gr} = 8.854$ m s$^{-1}$.
Least-speed case: $T_{\text{bot}} = 6mg = 6 \times 2 \times 9.8 = 117.6$ N.
At $5.0$ m s$^{-1}$ at the top: $T = m\left(\dfrac{v^2}{r} - g\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{5^2}{1.6} - 9.8\right) = 11.65$ N, a pull, so the rope is taut and the water stays in.

bullets: At $\varphi = 0$ (bottom): $6mg$. Level with the centre ($90^\circ$): $3mg$. At the top ($180^\circ$): zero.
The tension falls steadily all the way up, and reaches zero only at the top, exactly when the speed is the least possible.
Not examined: the ISC syllabus asks for the top and the bottom only. This curve just shows how those two results join up.

slides.narration: To sum up. On a level bend, friction supplies the force and the greatest speed is the square root of mu r g, whatever the mass. On a banked road, tan theta is v squared over r g, and a railway outer rail is raised by l sin theta. In a vertical circle, the least speed is root g r at the top and root five g r at the bottom, and the bottom tension is six m g more than the top.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Start with a free-body diagram of the **real** forces; then write one equation along the radius (towards the centre) and one perpendicular to it.
On a level road use $N = mg$ and $f = mv^2/r$; show that $m$ cancels in $v_{\max}$.
For banking write both equations, $N\cos\theta = mg$ and $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$, and divide; mention that the normal reaction is perpendicular to the **road**.
In the vertical circle write the radial equation at the top and at the bottom, and use energy conservation between them.

Common mistakes: using $\sqrt{gr}$ for the speed at the bottom; writing $T + mg$ at the bottom (there the weight points away from the centre, so $T - mg = mv^2/r$); forgetting to convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.

sections.heading: 1. Angular displacement, velocity and acceleration; relations with linear quantities
sections.body_md:
- **Angular displacement** $\theta$: the angle swept by the radius to the body; unit **radian**, $\theta = s/r$, so $s = r\theta$. $2\pi$ rad $= 360^\circ$, $1$ rad $= 57.30^\circ$. Anticlockwise is positive; the vector lies along the axis (right-hand rule).
- **Angular velocity** $\omega = \Delta\theta/\Delta t = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f$, in rad s$^{-1}$. rpm $\to$ rad s$^{-1}$: multiply by $2\pi/60$. A potter’s wheel at 75 rpm has $\omega = 7.854$ rad s$^{-1}$.
- **Linear speed** $v = r\omega$, along the tangent. All points of a rigid rotating body share one $\omega$; their speeds are proportional to their distances from the axis (0.3 m: 2.356 m s⁻¹; 0.1 m: 0.7854 m s⁻¹).
- **Angular acceleration** $\alpha = \Delta\omega/\Delta t$ in rad s$^{-2}$. For constant $\alpha$: $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$, $\theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2$. On an $\omega$–$t$ graph the slope is $\alpha$ and the area is $\theta$.
- **Tangential acceleration** $a_t = r\alpha$ (along the tangent; changes the speed). The radial part is the centripetal acceleration $a_c = \omega^2 r$. The total acceleration is $\sqrt{a_t^2 + a_c^2}$. Example: a fan tip at 0.6 m with $\alpha = 2.5$ rad s$^{-2}$ after 8 s has $\omega = 20.0$ rad s$^{-1}$, $a_t = 1.50$ m s$^{-2}$, $a_c = 240.0$ m s$^{-2}$.

sections.heading: 2. Centripetal acceleration; centripetal force as the name of a direction
sections.body_md:
- In **uniform circular motion** the speed is constant but the **velocity changes direction**, so the body has an acceleration.
- **Derivation.** Take points P and Q a small angle $\Delta\theta$ apart. Draw $\vec v_1$ and $\vec v_2$ (each of size $v$, perpendicular to its radius) from one point; the angle between them is $\Delta\theta$. $\Delta\vec v = \vec v_2 - \vec v_1$ is the base of an isosceles triangle: $|\Delta v| = 2v\sin(\Delta\theta/2) \approx v\Delta\theta$ for small $\Delta\theta$. So $a = |\Delta v|/\Delta t = v\omega = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$. As $\Delta\theta \to 0$, $\Delta\vec v$ is perpendicular to $\vec v$: **towards the centre**. Also $a = 4\pi^2 r/T^2$.
- **Scaling:** $a \propto v^2$ at fixed $r$; $a \propto 1/r$ at fixed $v$; $a \propto r$ at fixed $\omega$.
- **Centripetal force** $F = mv^2/r = m\omega^2 r$ is **the name of a direction**, not a new force. It is the net real force towards the centre: tension (stone on a string; the stone of 0.25 kg at 2 rev s$^{-1}$ on 0.8 m needs $T = 31.58$ N), static friction (coin on a turntable, car on a level bend), gravity (satellite), a normal reaction component (banked road). Never draw it as an extra force on a free-body diagram. It is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work.
- Example: a cyclist at 6.0 m s⁻¹ on a 12 m roundabout has $a = 3.00$ m s$^{-2}$; for 70 kg the force is 210 N, supplied by friction.

key_terms.definition_md: Motion on a circle at constant speed; the acceleration is purely centripetal.
The acceleration directed to the centre, a = v²/r = ω²r.
The name for the net real force directed to the centre, mv²/r; not a new force.

sections.heading: 3. Vehicle on a level circular road; banking of roads and railway tracks
sections.body_md:
- **Level road:** friction supplies the centripetal force; $N = mg$ and $mv^2/r \le \mu mg$, so $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu r g}$. The mass cancels. On a bend of radius 45 m: 17.57 m s⁻¹ when dry ($\mu = 0.7$), 12.42 m s⁻¹ when wet ($\mu = 0.35$).
- **Banked road** (outer edge higher; angle $\theta$): $N$ is perpendicular to the road. $N\cos\theta = mg$ and $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$, so **$\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$**, independent of the mass; the design speed is $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$. For 20 m s⁻¹ on 100 m: $\theta = 22.20^\circ$, and $N = mg/\cos\theta$ (8468 N for 800 kg). At the design speed no friction is needed.
- **Railway track:** the outer rail is raised by $h$ over a gauge $l$: $\sin\theta = h/l$, and for small $\theta$, $h \approx l v^2/(rg)$. For 20 m s⁻¹ on 500 m with $l = 1.676$ m: $h = 0.1364$ m. At other speeds the flange of the wheel presses on the outer rail (too fast) or the inner rail (too slow).
- On the banked road above the design speed a car tends to slide outwards, below it inwards; the extra force comes from friction.

sections.heading: 4. Motion in a vertical circle
sections.body_md:
- A ball on a string in a vertical circle has a **changing speed**: least at the top, greatest at the bottom. At every point, (force towards the centre) $= mv^2/r$.
- **Top:** $T + mg = mv^2/r$. A string cannot push, so $T \ge 0$; the **least speed** has $T = 0$: $v_{\text{top}} = \sqrt{gr}$. Slower, and the string goes slack.
- **Bottom:** $T - mg = mv^2/r$. Energy conservation from top to bottom (fall of $2r$): $v_{\text{bot}}^2 = v_{\text{top}}^2 + 4gr$, so the least speed at the bottom is $\sqrt{5gr}$.
- **Tensions:** $T_{\text{bot}} - T_{\text{top}} = 6mg$ for any speed; for the least speed, $T_{\text{top}} = 0$ and $T_{\text{bot}} = 6mg$. For 0.5 kg on 0.9 m: $\sqrt{gr} = 2.97$ m s⁻¹, $\sqrt{5gr} = 6.64$ m s⁻¹, $T_{\text{bot}} = 29.4$ N.
- A bucket of 2 kg on 1.6 m of rope at 5.0 m s⁻¹ at the top has $T = 11.65$ N (taut). The tension is greatest at the bottom, where a string is most likely to break.

key_terms.definition_md: v = √(gr), for which the tension is zero and the weight alone supplies the centripetal force.
v = √(5gr), needed to reach the top with the least speed there.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Convert rpm and km h⁻¹ to SI before using v = rω or v²/r.
- Uniform circular motion has acceleration v²/r towards the centre; derive it from the velocity triangle (|Δv| ≈ vΔθ).
- Centripetal force is not a new force: name the real force (tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction) and never draw it as an extra arrow.
- Level road: friction supplies mv²/r, so v_max = √(μrg), independent of mass.
- Banked road: N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r give tan θ = v²/(rg); the outer rail is raised by h = l sin θ.
- Vertical circle: top √(gr) (T = 0), bottom √(5gr), T_bottom − T_top = 6mg; write the radial equation at each point.

cards.front_md: Define one radian.
cards.back_md: The angle at the centre of a circle for which the arc length equals the radius; $\theta = s/r$.

cards.front_md: How many degrees are there in one radian?
cards.back_md: $1\ \text{rad} = 360^\circ/2\pi = 57.30^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Define angular velocity and give its SI unit.
cards.back_md: $\omega = d\theta/dt$; unit rad s$^{-1}$. For steady turning $\omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f$.

cards.front_md: State the direction of the angular velocity vector.
cards.back_md: Along the axis, given by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers the way the body turns, and the thumb points along $\omega$.

cards.front_md: Relate linear speed to angular speed.
cards.back_md: $v = r\omega$, along the tangent.

cards.front_md: Which quantities are the same for all points of a rotating rigid body?
cards.back_md: $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$ are the same; $v = r\omega$ and $a_t = r\alpha$ grow with $r$.

cards.front_md: Define angular acceleration.
cards.back_md: $\alpha = d\omega/dt$, in rad s$^{-2}$.

cards.front_md: Relate tangential acceleration to angular acceleration.
cards.back_md: $a_t = r\alpha$, along the tangent.

cards.front_md: Write the equations for rotation with constant $\alpha$.
cards.back_md: $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$ and $\theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2$.

cards.front_md: Convert 75 rpm to rad s$^{-1}$.
Why does a body in uniform circular motion have an acceleration?
cards.back_md: Its velocity changes direction continuously, although the speed is constant.

cards.front_md: Write the centripetal acceleration in three forms.
cards.back_md: $a = v^2/r = \omega^2 r = v\omega$; also $4\pi^2 r/T^2$.

cards.front_md: What is the direction of the centripetal acceleration, and why?
cards.back_md: Along the radius towards the centre: as $\Delta\theta \to 0$ the change in velocity becomes perpendicular to the velocity.

cards.front_md: In the velocity triangle, what is $|\Delta v|$?
cards.back_md: $|\Delta v| = 2v\sin(\Delta\theta/2) \approx v\Delta\theta$ for a small angle.

cards.front_md: How does the centripetal acceleration change if $v$ is doubled at the same radius?
cards.back_md: It becomes four times larger, since $a \propto v^2$.

cards.front_md: What is the centripetal force?
cards.back_md: The net real force directed towards the centre, $F = mv^2/r$. It is the name of a direction, not a new force.

cards.front_md: Which force supplies the centripetal force for a stone whirled on a string, a coin on a turntable and a satellite?
cards.back_md: Tension, static friction and gravity, respectively.

cards.front_md: Does the centripetal force do work in uniform circular motion?
cards.back_md: No: it is perpendicular to the velocity, so the speed does not change.

cards.front_md: Which force supplies the centripetal force for a car on a level curve?
cards.back_md: Static friction between the tyres and the road.

cards.front_md: Write the greatest speed of a car on a level circular road.
cards.back_md: $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu r g}$, independent of the mass of the car.

cards.front_md: Why is a road banked?
cards.back_md: So that the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force, and little or no friction is needed.

cards.front_md: Write the angle of banking for speed $v$ and radius $r$.
cards.back_md: $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$.

cards.front_md: Does the angle of banking depend on the mass of the vehicle?
cards.back_md: No: the mass cancels when $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$ is divided by $N\cos\theta = mg$.

cards.front_md: Why is the outer rail raised on a curved railway track?
cards.back_md: To bank the track so that the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force and the wheel flanges do not press sideways.

cards.front_md: Write the height by which the outer rail is raised.
cards.back_md: $h = l\sin\theta \approx l v^2/(rg)$, where $l$ is the gauge.

cards.front_md: What is the least speed at the top of a vertical circle on a string?
cards.back_md: $v = \sqrt{gr}$, for which the tension is zero.

cards.front_md: What is the least speed at the bottom of a vertical circle on a string?
cards.back_md: $v = \sqrt{5gr}$, from $v_{\text{bot}}^2 = v_{\text{top}}^2 + 4gr$.

cards.front_md: Write the radial equations at the top and the bottom.
cards.back_md: $T_{\text{top}} + mg = mv^2/r$ and $T_{\text{bot}} - mg = mv^2/r$.

cards.front_md: How much larger is the tension at the bottom than at the top?
cards.back_md: $6mg$, for any speed; at the least speed the top tension is 0 and the bottom tension is $6mg$.

questions.stem_md: A sprinter on a circular practice track of radius 40 m runs along the track for exactly 40 m. The angular displacement of the sprinter about the centre of the track is

1°, because the arc is 40 m
40 rad, the same number as the arc length
π rad, because the arc is as long as the radius times π

questions.solution_md: The angle in radians is the arc divided by the radius: 40 / 40 = 1 rad, which is one radian, about 57.3°.

questions.stem_md: A flywheel in a Nashik workshop turns anticlockwise when seen from above. By the right-hand rule, its angular velocity vector points

options.text_md: along the tangent at the rim, in the direction of motion of the rim
vertically upwards, along the axis of the flywheel
horizontally outwards from the axis, along a radius
vertically downwards, along the axis of the flywheel

questions.solution_md: Curling the fingers of the right hand in the sense of the turning (anticlockwise seen from above) makes the thumb point upwards. The angular velocity vector lies along the axis, not along the velocity of any particle.

questions.stem_md: Tanvi and Arjun ride a merry-go-round at a fair in Nagpur. Tanvi sits 1.5 m from the axis and Arjun 3 m from it. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Arjun has twice the angular velocity and the same speed as Tanvi
Both have the same angular velocity, and Arjun’s speed is twice Tanvi’s
Both have the same speed, and Arjun has half the angular velocity
Arjun has twice the angular velocity and twice the speed

questions.solution_md: The seats are fixed to one rigid platform, so all turn through the same angle in the same time: ω is the same. Then v = rω is proportional to r, and 3 / 1.5 = 2, so Arjun’s speed is twice Tanvi’s.

questions.stem_md: A ceiling fan in a Jaipur classroom turns at 240 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is

options.text_md: 4.0 rad s⁻¹
12.6 rad s⁻¹
1508 rad s⁻¹
25.1 rad s⁻¹

questions.solution_md: 240 revolutions in 60 s is 4 revolutions per second, and each revolution is 2π rad: ω = 4 × 2π = 25.13 rad s⁻¹. The numbers in the wrong options come from leaving out 2π, using π, or not dividing by 60.

questions.stem_md: A grinding wheel of radius 0.15 m speeds up with an angular acceleration of 12 rad s⁻². The tangential acceleration of a point on its rim is

options.text_md: 12 m s⁻², the same as the angular acceleration

questions.solution_md: The tangential acceleration is a_t = rα = 0.15 × 12 = 1.80 m s⁻². The wrong values come from dividing instead of multiplying, or from forgetting the radius.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The second hand of a big wall clock at Howrah station makes one complete turn in 60 s. Its angular velocity is

options.text_md: 6.28 rad s⁻¹
0.105 rad s⁻¹
0.0167 rad s⁻¹
1.05 rad s⁻¹

questions.solution_md: One turn is 2π rad and takes 60 s, so ω = 2π / 60 = 0.1047 rad s⁻¹, about 0.105 rad s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: Thiruvananthapuram lies close to the equator and Srinagar at a much higher latitude. Because of the rotation of the Earth about its axis

options.text_md: both cities have the same linear speed, because the Earth is a rigid body
Srinagar has the greater angular velocity, because it is nearer the pole
Srinagar has both the greater angular velocity and the greater linear speed
both cities have the same angular velocity, but Thiruvananthapuram has the greater linear speed

questions.solution_md: All points of the rigid Earth turn through the same angle each day, so ω is the same. The distance from the axis of rotation is greatest at the equator, and v = rω is proportional to it, so the city nearer the equator moves faster.

questions.stem_md: A stone tied to a thread is whirled in a horizontal circle at a constant speed. Its acceleration is

options.text_md: directed towards the centre of the circle, and constant in magnitude
zero, because the speed is constant
directed along the tangent, in the direction of motion
directed away from the centre of the circle

questions.solution_md: The speed is steady, but the velocity changes direction, so there is an acceleration. It points along the radius towards the centre, and its magnitude v²/r stays the same, while its direction keeps changing.

9 times as large
1.73 times as large
0.333 times as large

questions.solution_md: At a fixed radius and mass, F = mv²/r is proportional to v². Tripling the speed multiplies the force by 3² = 9.

questions.stem_md: Two small beads A and B are on a horizontal spoke that turns at a steady angular velocity about a vertical axis, at distances 0.1 m and 0.3 m from the axis. Bead B, compared with bead A, has

options.text_md: 3 times the speed and 9 times the centripetal acceleration
3 times the speed and 3 times the centripetal acceleration
the same speed and 3 times the centripetal acceleration
3 times the speed and one third of the centripetal acceleration

questions.solution_md: The angular velocity ω is the same for both. v = rω is proportional to r, so B’s speed is 3 times A’s. At fixed ω, a = ω²r is also proportional to r, so B’s centripetal acceleration is 3 times A’s, not 9 times.

questions.stem_md: A coin lies near the edge of a turntable at a village fair and turns with it, without slipping. The force that supplies the coin’s centripetal force is

options.text_md: the static friction of the turntable on the coin
the weight of the coin
the normal reaction of the turntable on the coin
a centrifugal force acting on the coin, pointing outwards

questions.solution_md: The weight and the normal reaction are vertical and balance each other. The only horizontal force on the coin is the friction of the turntable, and it points to the centre: it is the force that plays the role of the centripetal force. There is no outward force on the coin.

questions.stem_md: A student draws the free-body diagram of a stone whirled on a string over a smooth table. She shows two inward arrows on the stone: the tension T, and another arrow labelled “centripetal force mv²/r”. The best comment is that

options.text_md: the diagram is correct, because both forces act on the stone
the second arrow counts the same inward force twice: mv²/r only gives the size of the net inward force, which here is the tension alone
the second arrow should point outwards, away from the centre
the diagram is correct, but the tension should be drawn along the tangent

questions.solution_md: Centripetal force is the name of a direction, not an extra force. The only real horizontal force is the tension, and Newton’s second law says that this net inward force equals mv²/r. Drawing both double-counts it.

questions.stem_md: A stone whirled anticlockwise (seen from above) in a horizontal circle on a string is at the northmost point of its circle when the string snaps. The stone then moves

options.text_md: towards the centre of the circle, southwards
in a straight line along the tangent, towards the west
away from the centre, northwards
along a curved path, continuing the same circle

questions.solution_md: With the string gone there is no horizontal force, so the stone keeps the velocity it had: tangential to the circle. For anticlockwise motion the velocity at the northmost point is towards the west.

questions.stem_md: In the velocity triangle for uniform circular motion, the angle Δθ between the velocities at two nearby points is made smaller and smaller. The change in velocity Δv then

options.text_md: tends to point along the tangent, in the direction of the velocity
tends to point away from the centre of the circle
tends to point towards the centre of the circle
tends to become equal to v in size

questions.solution_md: The base angles of the isosceles triangle are 90° − Δθ/2, which approaches 90°. So Δv becomes perpendicular to v, that is along the radius, and its sense is towards the centre. Its size, about vΔθ, tends to zero.

questions.stem_md: A scooter turns round a flat curve at a Kochi junction. The force that supplies its centripetal force is

options.text_md: the weight of the scooter and rider
the normal reaction of the road
the driving force of the engine
the static friction between the tyres and the road

questions.solution_md: On a level road the weight and the normal reaction are vertical. The engine force is along the motion. The only horizontal force pointing to the centre is the sideways friction of the road on the tyres.

questions.stem_md: An empty lorry can take a level bend safely at a greatest speed of 15 m s⁻¹. After loading so that its mass is doubled, the greatest safe speed on the same bend (same tyres and road) is

options.text_md: still 15 m s⁻¹
30 m s⁻¹
7.5 m s⁻¹

questions.solution_md: The friction needed, mv²/r, and the greatest friction available, μmg, are both proportional to the mass. The mass cancels in v_max = √(μrg), so doubling it changes nothing.

marking_scheme.step: v_max = √(μrg) does not contain the mass: still 15 m s⁻¹ (a)

questions.stem_md: On a dry road with μ = 0.64, the greatest safe speed on a level curve is 16 m s⁻¹. In heavy rain μ falls to 0.16. The greatest safe speed on the same curve becomes
questions.solution_md: Since v_max = √(μrg), v is proportional to √μ. μ falls to one quarter, so v falls to one half: 16 × √(0.16/0.64) = 8.00 m s⁻¹, not one quarter.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A car goes round a banked bend at the design speed, so that no friction is needed. The centripetal force on it is supplied by

options.text_md: the whole of the normal reaction of the road
the horizontal component of the weight of the car
the component of the weight along the road
the horizontal component of the normal reaction of the road
